paper_design_summary: Twenty people (13 professional UX designers, the others enrolled in design-related programs) were recruited and asked to complete two 10-minute Miro design sprints, one with the GPT-4 CPD plugin and one without; all except one completed both, and P15 completed only the no-plugin sprint (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.2; p. 16, Appendix A, Table 1). The supervised remote study used Zoom, with plugin-condition and sprint order randomized within person (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3). Paired sample t-tests compared self-reported ease and confidence, time on task, and the number of pathways in each diagram (p. 7, Section 4.4).

studies.label: Within-subjects user study (two design sprints, with and without the CPD plugin)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the plugin and no-plugin conditions (and the order of the two design sprints) within each participant
assignment.quote: For one of the design sprints, participants were given the plugin to help generate CPDs. In the other design sprint, they were not given the plugin. We randomized the order in which a participant would use the plugin

arms.name: With plugin
arms.description: Miro CPD plugin with drag-and-drop components, a step-by-step Wizard, GPT-4 brainstorming suggestions, checking, and help

arms.name: Without plugin
arms.description: Same CPD design sprint in Miro without the plugin

participants.exclusions: One of 20 participants left early and completed only the no-plugin sprint, so at most 19 people have both sprints. The paper does not state the n for the pathway-count test. The self-report tests print t(18) and t(17).
participants.who: 13 professional UX designers and 7 people enrolled in design-related programs, recruited through a screener survey on social media; none knew causal pathway diagrams before the study
participants.quote: we were able to recruit 20 people to participate in our study. ... All participants except one completed both design sprints.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 (temperature 1, max_tokens 256) inside a custom Miro plugin
ai_tool.how_used: Wizard and Brainstorming features recommend candidate content for diagram components on request; the plugin also has non-AI features (component templates, checking, glossary)

task.description: Design sprint: given a design prompt, persona, and scenario, build a causal pathway diagram to ideate possible solutions

outcomes.name: Number of CPD pathways generated in the sprint
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of pathways in each participant's diagram; paired sample t-test

contrasts.reported: M_without_plugin = 1.47 vs. M_with_plugin = 2.32; p < .05 (Figure 4b shows standard-error bars)

eligibility.reason: Randomized within-person order of a GPT-4 plugin versus no plugin (p. 6, Section 4.1), but only 20 people were recruited and at most 19 completed both conditions (p. 6, Section 4.2), well below 50. The only output-scored outcome is the pathway count; the creativity claim otherwise rests on self-reports and interviews. The plugin bundles non-AI features with the GPT-4 suggestions. Listed in the screening report as a small randomized experiment.

one_line_finding: With the GPT-4 plugin, designers drew more causal pathways in a 10-minute sprint than without it (2.32 vs. 1.47, p < .05; p. 9, Section 5.2.1), with about the same time (556 s vs. 603 s, p > 0.5).

applied.old: Twenty designers (13 professional UX designers, the rest design students) each did two 10-minute online design sprints, drawing causal pathway diagrams in Miro, once with a plugin that includes GPT-4 suggestions and once without it. The order of the plugin condition and of the sprints was randomized within person. The paper compares self-reported ease and confidence, time on task, and the number of pathways in each diagram with paired t-tests.
